title: Run a spring-hinge deployment test with the hinge turned gravity-neutral
instruction: Run a bench deployment test of the gold solar-panel dummy: pull the red hold-down pin so its light hinge spring alone opens it to its latch, then let go. The spring is a flight spring, sized for orbit.
context: Turn a mechanism so gravity no longer acts along its motion before setting it off. Unlike turning a rollover fixture to reach a far face (TK-XLTXT8) or freeing a fire door for its closer (TK-VNC9LD), the turn here reaches and unblocks nothing: it is needed only because gravity would beat the flight spring. Aerospace engineering and operations technicians (O*NET 17-3021.00) and avionics technicians (49-2091.00) run ground deployment tests of CubeSat solar-panel and antenna hinges. Flight springs are sized for zero g and cannot lift a panel against gravity, so the hinge is turned axis-vertical on a tilt fixture and the panel swings in a horizontal plane. A test released in the wrong orientation, or helped by hand, is invalid. This is honest 1 g bench practice; no microgravity is claimed.
setup: Station table; positions in metres, x forward from the arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up; the table top is at z 0.7475. (1) Tilt fixture stand, fixed to the table, 3.5 kg: a grey cast-iron foot 140 x 90 x 10 mm, sRGB (0.45, 0.46, 0.48), centred at (0.330, 0.150), and a dark grey painted cast-iron worm gearbox column 70 x 70 x 130 mm, sRGB (0.30, 0.31, 0.33), centred at (0.330, 0.150), top at z 0.8875, with a 36 mm trunnion bearing boss on its right face at (0.330, 0.110, 0.8575). (2) Crank on the column top, on a dark grey steel input-shaft bearing post 20 mm across and 6 mm tall, 50 g, sRGB (0.30, 0.31, 0.33): black steel, sRGB (0.10, 0.10, 0.11), 60 g, vertical axis at (0.330, 0.150); a 24 mm hub and a 40 mm arm of 12 x 6 mm section at z 0.8945 to 0.9005, pointing toward the robot at the start; a black acetal handle sleeve 16 mm across and 30 mm tall, 10 g, free to turn, centred at (0.290, 0.150, 0.9175). Crank friction 0.03 N m, damping 0.01 N m s/rad. It drives the trunnion through a self-locking 12:1 worm: one turn anticlockwise seen from above tilts the table 30 deg, its top face turning away from the robot, between stops at 0 and 95 deg. (3) Tilt table (cradle): natural aluminium plate 120 x 170 x 8 mm, sRGB (0.76, 0.77, 0.79), 0.45 kg, cantilevered from the column on a 20 mm trunnion shaft along y whose axis is 110 mm above the table at x 0.330, z 0.8575; the plate is centred on the axis from y -0.095 to 0.075, top at z 0.8615 as delivered; an aluminium pin bracket 16 x 15 x 17 mm on its right end (y -0.093 to -0.078); two aluminium hinge knuckles 8 mm across and 30 mm long on the hinge line at x 0.295 and 0.365. (4) Gold panel: a 1U-size deployable solar-panel dummy, aluminium honeycomb board with a gold-coloured face, sRGB (0.85, 0.68, 0.22), 100 x 120 x 4 mm, 150 g with its centre of mass at the board's centre, friction 0.5 / 0.4, stowed flat on the cradle 0.5 mm above it and centred at (0.330, -0.005, 0.864). Its spring hinge runs along x at its left edge (y 0.055, z 0.862): a flight torsion spring of 0.0191 N m/rad preloaded to 0.050 N m stowed and 0.020 N m at 90 deg, a viscous damper of 0.008 N m s/rad, 0.003 N m friction, a 90 deg hard stop and a latch pawl that drops in at 89 deg. A gold hinge knuckle 8 mm across and 38 mm long sits between the cradle's two, and a 14 x 8 x 16 mm hold-down boss with a 4 mm slot on its right end. (5) Red hold-down pin: a 3 mm steel pull rod, 75 mm long, engaged 6 mm in the boss's slot through the bracket, with a red nylon pull knob 12 mm across and 16 mm long, sRGB (0.85, 0.08, 0.08), centred at (0.330, -0.150, 0.870) as delivered; 15 g; it slides 0 to 20 mm along -y on 0.5 N of friction, and 8 mm out it frees the panel.
scoring: Measured every control step from reset: the hinge axis's angle from vertical (from the cradle's pose), the fixture tilt, the pin's pull, the panel's hinge angle q and the latch, each gripper's pad clearance to the panel and to the fixture's moving parts, gripper speeds, and the panel's speed and spin from its pose change between control steps. Whole-run record (a linkkit History plus the release record, updated every control step and cleared only by the simulator reset). Release gate: the hold-down lets go when the pin first passes 8 mm; that release is recorded once with the axis angle at that moment. Gates, giving 0 for the run: the release was made with the hinge axis more than 10 deg from vertical (an invalid test: as delivered the spring fights gravity), or any gripper pad came within 5 mm of the panel at any time after the release (an assisted deployment). Ladder: 0.25 = the hinge axis was within 10 deg of vertical at some time; 0.5 = a valid release; 0.75 = after it the panel reached its latch (89 deg); 1.0 = also at the end the panel is latched (88 deg or more), the axis still within 10 deg of vertical, the panel still (under 3 mm/s and 3 deg/s) for 1 s, and the let-go gate: every pad point of both grippers at least 30 mm from the cradle, panel, pin, crank and handle and both grippers moving under 5 mm/s for the last 1 s. Success (1.0) must hold 1 s. Real trial: a protractor or inclinometer on the tilt table and the hinge, a scale on the pin, and the video for the release, any touch and the latch.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Swing the panel back flat onto the cradle (lift the latch pawl first) and push the red pin home through the bracket into the boss's slot, 6 mm engaged, knob 47 mm past the cradle's end. Turn the crank clockwise until the tilt table stops at 0 deg (top face up, hinge axis horizontal), then on until the arm points toward the robot. The stand is fixed on taped outlines and needs no reset.
fidelity: Rigid links. The worm is a stiff tilt drive whose target follows the crank angle (12:1, 30 deg per turn, coarse to fit the run; it never back-drives the crank; past 0 or 95 deg the crank turns freely). The hold-down is a hinge brake released once the pin is 8 mm out, not a pin load. Linear torsion spring and damper; the latch is a pawl limit. No offload rig. A 1 g bench analogue; no microgravity is claimed.
